Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Vignette:
Kofi was forty-six years old, a park ranger in a sprawling national forest in the Pacific Northwest, a job he had held for nearly a decade after leaving the Army. He was married to a woman named Amara, a nurse who worked long shifts, and they had two teenage daughters. When he first described the event that had brought him to therapy, he did so with his eyes fixed on a corner of the room, his voice flat. It had happened during a deployment in the Horn of Africa, a routine supply convoy that had turned into an ambush in a narrow wadi. He had been the gunner in a lead vehicle. The fight had lasted less than four minutes, but the sound of the helicopter that had been scrambled for extraction—its rotors thudding overhead as they loaded the wounded—had lodged itself somewhere deep in his skull. What he remembered most vividly now, years later, was not the gunfire itself but the smell: hot dust, cordite, and the sharp, metallic tang of blood. When he tried to describe it to his therapist, he said the memory felt more real than ordinary things, as though he could reach out and touch the heat of that afternoon. The images were clear and detailed, almost photographic, but they came without warning, pulling him out of the present and dropping him back into that wadi.

In the months after the ambush, Kofi had told himself that he had to move on, that the Army had trained him for this. But the sense that he had permanently changed for the worse had settled into him like a bone-deep ache. He was certain that he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened—for not seeing the signs earlier, for not being faster. He had come to believe that he had to be on guard all the time, because if he let his attention slip, something terrible would happen again. At first, this vigilance had seemed like a survival skill, something that kept him alive. But it had bled into everything. At work, he would find himself scanning the treeline for signs of danger even when he was leading a simple nature hike. He watched other people closely, studying their hands and their eyes, trying to read whether they might harm him. A hiker who stepped too suddenly onto the trail could make him freeze. Unexpected or loud sounds—a car backfiring, a branch snapping underfoot—would spike his heart rate and leave him breathless, his vision narrowing.

The worst moments came without any obvious trigger. He would be standing at the ranger station, talking to a visitor about trail conditions, and a feeling of being uncomfortable would creep over him, a skin-crawling restlessness that made him want to flee. Sometimes it deepened into something worse: a dissociative feeling, as though he were beginning to detach from his own body, watching himself from a distance. He had learned to force himself to stay still, to keep his face neutral, but the effort exhausted him. And then there were the sounds that hit him hardest. The park used a small helicopter for fire surveillance and search-and-rescue operations. Whenever Kofi heard its rotors in the distance, a cold dread would wash over him. He would stop whatever he was doing and listen, his jaw tight, until the sound faded. He had started to arrange his patrol routes to stay as far as possible from the helipad, telling his supervisor it was just a preference for the quieter trails. His colleagues had noticed that he was jumpy, that he sometimes flinched at nothing, but they attributed it to his military background—a veteran’s quirks, they said. They did not know that he spent his evenings in the garage, sitting in his truck in the dark, because the silence of the house made the memories louder.

The consequences had accumulated slowly. He had stopped going to family gatherings at Amara’s parents’ house because the noise and the sudden movements of children made him feel trapped. He had stopped answering calls from his old Army friends. His daughters had learned not to startle him, and that knowledge—that they had to tiptoe around their own father—had become a quiet grief in the household. Amara had begun to ask him, gently, whether he was okay, and he had said yes every time, because he did not have words for what was happening. What finally brought him to seek help was a morning in the park when a group of teenagers had set off a firecracker near the visitor center. Kofi had dropped to a crouch behind a picnic table, his hand reaching for a weapon that was not there, and a family had seen him. They had stared. His supervisor had pulled him aside and suggested, not unkindly, that he take some leave. Kofi had driven home and sat in the garage for an hour, and then he had called a number from a veterans’ resource card he had kept in his wallet for three years. He was afraid that he was losing his grip on the life he had built, and he was hoping, though he could not quite say it aloud, that someone could help him find a way back to himself.
